Mr. Speaker, at six
o'clock I had read letters from several of the provincial premiers in reply to my communication accompanying a copy of the report of the Commission on Industrial Training and Technical Education, and expressing a desire that they should give me the benefit of their views on the recommendations contained in that report. I have one or two further letters to read. On May 6, 1914, not having had any reply from the Premier of Manitoba, my deputy wrote him as follows:
Dear Sir,-The Honourable Mr. Crothers, Minister of Labour, has requested me to remind you of the letter he addressed you under date of March 12, referring to the report of the Royal Commission on Industrial Training and Technical Education, a copy of which, comprising four volumes, was addressed to you on that date. The minister's letter, a copy of which is enclosed, has perhaps escaped your attention in the press of public matters, but the minister asks me to say that he would be obliged if you could at your earliest con-

vcnience give him the benefit of your views on the subject therein discussed.
On May 11, 1914, we received the following communication, addressed to the Deputy Minister of Labour:
I have your letter of May 6, also copy of the letter of the Honourable Mr. Crothers of March 12, 1914. The volumes of the report of the Royal Commission were received, but I am willing to admit that I have not read them. While interested in industrial training and technical education, yet I have so many other things to engage my attention that 1 have not so far had the time to read the report, and consequently cannot give my opinion. I presume, however, that the report is one that deals with the matter is a comprehensive and educational way, and, being made by professional men, would scarcely admit of any review by myself that would be of advantage to the department. I shall read the report, however, at my earliest convenience.
That is the last communication that we have from the Premier of Manitoba. These replies, with thq exception of one, do not, I think, manifest any burning desire that the recommendations of this commission should be immediately adopted. I am sorry to say that, with one exception, they do not manifest that interest in the subject which I think its merit demands. It is a very important subject, and it does not appear to interest many people as much as it should. I noticed this afternoon, when the hon. member for Rouville was making a very able and eloquent address on this question and pressing its importance on the House, that he had behind him a mere baker's dozen, by actual count. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot congratulate myself on having secured a larger attendance on this side of the House.
The report about which we have been speaking consists of four large volumes, covering 2,350 pages. It contains much information in great detail; it has probably never yet been read throughout by any one. It recommends that this Government should provide annually the sum of $3,350,000 during a period of ten years, to be distributed among the nine provinces on the basis of population, to assist them in establishing a system of technical education and industrial training. It recommends an elaborate scheme for carrying out this work, involving the constitution of a Dominion development conference, a Dominion development commission, a Dominion development fund, a provincial development commission, a provincial development council, local urban industrial development boards, and local rural development boards-a scheme most complicated, and, I believe, utterly impracticable of execution. Beyond
the receipt of these replies of the Provincial Premiers, no official communication has been received from any one of them.
Did my hon. friend receive a reply from the Quebec Government?

Yes, I have read it. This does not indicate, I think, any enthusiastic desire on their part for the adoption of the recommendations contained in this report. I have personal knowledge that several of the provinces strongly object to the adoption of this scheme. Our people are very jealous of provincial rights. Those of us who come from Ontario know that for 15 or 20 years, the two great political parties in that province were quarrelling over a very small matter of provincial rights. Our people are jealous of provincial rights; especially are they extremely sensitive on the question of education, differences concerning which ever since Confederation have retarded the progress of influences tending and intended to strengthen the bonds of unity, friendship and confidence among the chief races and creeds composing our population, and have caused more heartburnings and enmities than any others. So that it seems to me that it would be extremely unwise to enter on any national scheme of education such as is recommended in this report until we are quite sure that it contains no provision the carrying out of which might by any possibility arouse jealousies, passions, and discords, so much to be deprecated and avoided. In the several provinces much work of this character has already been done, and I am of the opinion that the details in carrying it forward should be left to them. We cannot be too careful to guard the rights of the provinces exclusively and clearly assigned them by the constitution.
In nearly all the provinces much good work has already been done in this direction, sometimes by municipalities, sometimes by the provincial government. In the city of Toronto they have just completed a technical school at a cost of $2,000,000, said to be the finest technical school in Canada. They have already secured sites in the city of Toronto for four branches to be built in the outer parts of the city. In the province of Ontario, under the statutes of 1911, and 1913, there are 34 centres where they are imparting technical education. I am not so familiar with the province of Quebec, but I do know that the Government of Quebec is maintaining two excellent technical schools, one at Quebec city, and one at Montreal.

So there is a good deal of very valuable work being done along these lines in the various provinces, sometimes by the provinces themselves, and at other times by the municipalities. I would be very glad, so far as I am concerned, to render any assistance within our power as soon as our finances warrant such a step. Personally I do not think that they do warrant such a step at the present time. The provinces are getting on very well. It is not a matter that you can rush through in a few days, or a few months, or in a year or two; it,is a matter of growth. My hon. friend referred to the technical schools in Germany. I wish he could have found some other country to refer to. I do not say that one thing followed the other, but while the Germans were becoming so efficient technically, the finer qualities of their minds and hearts seem to have been paralysed, so that they were capable of the atrocities of which they have been convicted in Belgium, and which will stamp them with infamy for ages to come. I do not say that these things resulted from technical schools, but they resulted from a system of education of one side of the human being, which left uneducated the finer and nobler qualities of mind and heart.
This resolution calls upon us to give effect to the report of the commission at the earliest possible opportunity, and it refers to the recommendations contained in the report. The Commission was appointed for the purpose of getting information for the provinces. It was not admitted by this Parliament that we had anything to do with the matter; on the contrary it was declared that we would have nothing to do with it. The commission was not authorized to make any such recommendations, or to express any such opinions, they were authorized to' gather information, I have said, which is the fact, that the Order in Council, and the commission , following it, wont further than the letters which were sent to .the various {Prime Minister warranted. I think the proper influence was that the recommendations and opinions invited, were to be, not the 'basis of any action by this Parliament, but the basis of action by the various provinces. The provincial governments have said, in .substance, .that they do not want this; that is the fair inference from the replies received from eight out of the nine. With the exceptions of Nova Scotia they say: we do not approve of those recommendations, and yet my hon. friend's

motion asks us to give effect to them. Personally I know that several of them do not approve of them; therefore, I think we will have no difficulty in saying that at the present time we should not adopt the motion presented to this House by my hon. friend from Rouville.

Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend the Minister of Labour had finished his remarks before six o'clock, I think that ten minutes would have been sufficient to enable me to answer what he said. He has spent a good deal of time reading letters sent to the premiers of the different provinces, and the answers received, but to my mind, they have nothing whatever to do with this question. In his concluding remarks he stated that the resolution as presented must either be killed, or carried exactly as it is. He stated that he would be willing to do something if possible. If the report of the commission recommends that $3,000,000 per year be granted for ten years, is the minister willing to vote half a million dollars for all the provinces. Where is the provincial government that would not be satisfied with whatever grant this Parliament saw fit to give at the present time? It is not so much a question of amount as it is a question of principle. The idea of technical education forms probably the only ground upon which employers and employees stand unitedly. It is not often that you hear in this House of employers and employees meeting on common ground but on the question of the desirability of promoting technical education they are united. They are united upon this question because they know that the great producers of wealth must have a better technical education. If I understand rue motion my hon. friend from Rouville has brought before the House, even during the war, its underlying idea is that the wealth producing power of the people of Canada must be developed in such a way that when this war is over we will be able to produce three or four times as much as we have ever been able to produce before.
It is acknowledged that every one has a certain amount of brain power and that it only awaits development. This development is dependent upon education. If it were not for brain power the Allies would never win this war. We must not only have physical power but we must have brain power as well. I believe that the Government should be willing to do something to promote this movement for tech-

nical education. I feel sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) would be willing to assist in this direction. The Government ought to do something to assist the schools already in existence in the different provinc&s to enable them to do a little more than they have done in the past. I. was a member of the board of directors of the Montreal Technical School for three years and a half and I know what we have to put up with. But, we are doing the very best we can. The principal of that school told me only last week that during all his experience in France he has never found as high a degree of brain power amongst those with whom he had dealt in that country as he found amongst the Canadian boys in his school, and it is a bilingual school, if you please. When he says " Canadian " he does not say " French-Canadian," but he uses the word " Canadian " in the right sense. He says that the pupils are endowed with brains but all they require is a -little education. It has been impossible, so far, not only in the province of Quebec, but in the other provinces of Canada, to do the work that ought to have been done along that line. Let us suppose that a definite proposition was made to grant $100,000, or $50,000, to the province of Ontario, or a proportionate amount, according to population, to the province of Quebec, do you' suppose that these Governments would refuse it? No. I agree with my hon. friend when he states that if the money is granted it should be granted as a subsidy and that the Federal Government should have it so fixed that the money cannot be spent for anything else but technical education. I do not believe that any Provincial Government would refuse to accept the money on those terms.
The producing power of this country is going to be greatly diminished after the war. Many of the men who left to go to the front will never come back. We will have to rely on those who are here, on the young men especially, who are going to these schools, and who cannot go to the war because they are too young. These young men, after having had the benefit of technical education, and when they reach the age of 18, are in great demand. We have proved that, not only in Montreal, but wherever there are technical schools. In Montreal we have more demands for boys who have passed their examinations than we can comply with. The parents and relations of many of these boys are frequently
not in a position to send them to technical schools. A federal grant might be devoted to providing purses in order that the poor boy might receive the education that he desires. It is quite a drain on the resources of some of the parents to pay the school fees. In Montreal we never refuse any one who is unable to pay the fees. If these payments were exacted in every instance it would frequently be found to be beyond the power of the father of a large family to send his boys to a school of this kind. If there was a certain amount granted that we could apply to purses we could put 200 more boys through that course every year in the city of Montreal.
My hon. friend from Rouville does not propose in his resolution that every letter of the report which was laid before the House a couple of years ago shall be immediately put into effect. I do not believe it was his intention that effect should be given to the report in its entirety. The Minister of Labour would be willing to do something, to grant something, he says, if the times favoured it. During war, when we are spending money lavishly, it means a mere bagatelle to spend a few hundred thousand dollars for technical education. We have been juggling with millions in the last year or two and we say we are doing so because we want to win the war.
Germany has been mentioned in this dis-cusion. If the brain power of the German working men had been developed in the right direction probably there would have been no war. We do not intend to follow the example of Germany in this matter; we intend to direct the minds of the younger generation in another channel altogether. The Minister of Labour cannot excuse his failure to take action by saying that my hon. friend from Rouville will not accept anything but what is in his motion. The fact is absolutely the reverse. The present Government might vote, we will say, $1,000,000. That would be $1,000,000 for technical education in Canada to be divided between the different provinces according to population. It would mean that in three years from to-day you would have probably 300, 400 or 500 first-class mechanics, equipped with a high degree of technical knowledge in the different industries in the country. We have had in the past, I am sorry to say, to go to the old country to get professors of different kinds. The acquisition of technical knowledge has been very badly neglected in this country for a great many years. It is something

new with us. We are a new country. We sometimes hear it said in this House that we are the greatest producing country in the world, that we are the richest country in the world, that we have greater natural resources than any other country in the world. But, I ask, what are we going to do to develop these resources? Are we going to continue to send to the old country 'to get professors to educate our boys?
Anybody who has read history-if I may be allowed to speak of that country-knows there are some pretty good men in Germany. There are some good labour men in Germany. If they are fighting it is because they have to and not because they like it. But, I say that anybody who has read history knows that after the Franco-Prussian war of 1870, if it had not been for technical education in Germany, they would never have produced the instruments of war that have come into use in the present struggle. Our position is absolutely different. We 'are going to be called upon to produce raw material and finished products of all kinds for the world. If we are called upon to do this after the war we will have to spend large sums of money to get professors from the old country to come and educate our boys in the different industrial arts. Why not pay the money ' now and try to have our boys ready for the task when the time comes? That is all I have to say on this question. I am simply asking the Government, if they cannot adopt the report in its entirety, if they cannot give $3,000,000 to at least give one million or five hundred thousand dollars. They could save that half million dollars in one contract if they wanted to. I urge the Government to study this question ana, if possible, to make a grant; but if they do, I insist upon the Government's seeing that the money is spent on nothing else but technical education.

It seems to me it would be very unfortunate if this debate were left exactly where it is, because the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve might leave the impression that there is hostility on the part of some one in this House towards technical education. Such, of course, is not the case. We have heard not only today, but on previous days, the highest possible praise of technical education, and of the report that has been made on the subject. The argument this afternoon and evening really centres upon the feasibility
fMr. Verville.]
of some plan of assisting the provinces. I admit that it -would appear to be a churlish thing to reject such a resolution as has been moved by the hon. member for Rou-ville; and it is not the intention to reject the principle involved. A way out has been suggested by the hon. member for Maisonneuve, who says that unquestionably the hon. member for Rouville would not insist upon the precise'wording of his resolution. I would therefore suggest, in accordance with the suggestion of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve, that this resolution be withdrawn and a new one prepared, on which we will have -a debate on some other day. I am sure my hon. friend from Maisonneuve will agree that that is a pleasant way out of the difficulty, considering that the difficulty is that we must not force our opinions on the provinces.

A few nights ago I took the opportunity of saying a few words on this subject, when it came up in a somewhat different form. I am in the anomalous position of having spoken in favour of technical education, which has my profound sympathy, and yet feeling myself unable to-night to support the resolution of the hon. member for Rou-vi'lle (Mr. Lemieux) as it has been presented to the House; and I am unable to support it largely by reason of the explanation given by the Minister of Labour this afternoon, and as a result of hearing the correspondence between the Department of Labour and the Premiers of the various provinces. Tbe hon. member for Maisonneuve said that the provinces would willingly take any grant this Government chose to make, and suggested that the grant be in proportion to the population. I am not in sympathy with that idea as regards technical education, for I believe that the necessary foundation for its success is a close personal interest in the subject by the provinces, which, of course, have control of our educational system. We all know that after the provinces had organized a system of aid to agriculture in their continuation schools, and after district representatives had been supplied to the various counties interested in this form of assistance, the Dominion Government set aside a certain 3om of money for technical education as applied to agriculture. And I think in this matter of technical education as applied to agriculture, we should proceed on practically the same basis, and assist those provinces that are

taking .an interest in the subject themselves. If the provinces are not aroused to the need of technical education within their own borders, and are not interested themselves in the subject, I cannot see how any grant by this Government would encourage an interest that does not exist. I am very much surprised at the attitude of the province of Ontario, and the other provinces that have not responded to the call, or it might even be said the offer, that went out from this Government. Ontario is on record as being favourably disposed towards technical education in all its branches. I think I am correct in saying that in no other province has technical education made such great headway, or have such large grants been made towards schools for the purpose of developing technical education. The province of Ontario years ago committed itself to technical education as applied to agriculture. Only the other day I saw in the newspaper that the Premier of Ontario and the leader of the Opposition both expressed strong sympathy with this movement. Of course, they were referring particularly to that phase of the subject which was introduced in this House by the hon. member for Pictoii (Mr. Macdonald) a week or so ago, that is, technical education to enable disabled soldiers to earn their livelihood in occupations different from those they formerly followed. The Toronto Globe, March 4, speaking of certain correspondence with reference to the conference of Provincial Premiers, that Premier Bearst had been asked to bring down, says:
The conference referred to was called by the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, last fall. Every province but British Columbia was represented by one or more of its cabinet ministers. British Columbia could not send a representative, because the distance was too great to allow one to reach Ottawa in time. The attitude taken from first to last was that the war was a national undertaking. The provinces, however, decided to co-operate and do everything in their power to assist the Dominion with war work and the care of returned disabled soldiers. They had had a conference later with the Dominion Hospitals Commission, and the final understanding arrived at was that a memorandum should be prepared, agreeable to all concerned, outlining the duties and responsibilities of the provincial governments in this matter.
The education and equipment of soldiers who would come back from the front to enable them to do work they were not equipped for before the war was one of the things the provincial government had in mind.
"We understand and appreciate how very important it is that we should make every provision we can for training the soldier who comes back unfitted for his previous work," said the Premier, who went on to tell of good
work already being done in the Toronto Technical School. A former bricklayer had come back from the war minus an arm, and in the technical school he was taking a course in order that he might fill the position of clerk of the work with a firm of contractors. Thus he would be able to earn as much, and perhaps more, than he received as a bricklayer.
It is hard to reconcile that statement with the position the Ontario Government has taken' towards technical education in the correspondence the Minister of Labour has read this afternoon.	.
I notice in this evening's Ottawa Citizen an editorial on some remarks of Viscount Haldane. The title of the article is " Preparedness for Peace," and Viscount Haldane has well said that it is the duty of the Government to prepare for peace as well as for war and that, if we do.not look to the needs of our artisans in respect to technical education, it may be that even after the conclusion of the war, if it be prolonged, we may find ourselves equally as unprepared in technical work to compete with those countries which have devoted so much time and money to the development of technical education as we found ourselves unprepared in regard to munitions of war. The editorial says in part:
Viscount Haldane, former British Secretary for War, in addressing a meeting at the University of Liverpool, stated that he. was more afraid of an engine for conquest in peace time, which the Germans were constructing before the war, than of any of their 42 centimetre guns. This engine was educational, and Viscount Haldane declared it to he the most modern form of continuation work, which was spreading over a large part of Germany. It consisted of school work for imparting trade skill and general knowledge. Germany, in short, had begun to train the youth of the land in special skilled trades to out-distance competitors throughout the world.
The subject of technical education was under discussion in the British House of Commons on the 10th of January last, and the hon. member for Rouville this afternoon quoted some passages from the remarks of several eminent gentlemen who spoke on that occasion. I notice that Mr. Lynch, speaking on the subject towards the close of the debate, said:
I propose to say a few words on a subject which, although it has not been much dealt with in the course of the debate, underlies it all, and that is the question of technical education. In the course of the debate, which has been highly interesting and instructive, the president of the Board of Trade recited several instances where Germany had built up great industries, some of them on the basis of inventions which had emanated either from this country or from France, and he cited in particular the industries of the aniline dyes, of
The whole thing cost about $120,000.

To think that the Dominion Government should have spent $120,000 to gather that information, and that some of the provinces gave every encouragement to this Government to collect this information for them, and then, when it was collected and printed, and presented to them, they should display absolutely no interest in it, and should not have courtesy enough even to reply to the correspondence, it is not creditable to the provinces. They apparently do not feel the responsibility that rests upon them, and when they have not that feeling of responsibility it would not be consistent or advisable for this Government to try to force upon them a grant of money for such purposes. I am sorry that the provinces have assumed this attitude. I am sorry they are not alive to the very great importance of this subject. I believe, as the minister has said, that the one and serious object that confronts us to-day is the winning of this war for freedom and liberty. I believe it is our duty, so far ais it is within our power, to prepare our engines for peace in time of war; and the best engine we can prepare to meet the attack of Gennan competition in commerce when this war is over, will be the better equipment of our
2306 \___

men. Why, Sir, we know, as a matter oi fact, that in Canadians we have better material to work on, a better spirit, better minds, more capable men in every respect than they have in Germany. All that is needed is to give our people opportunity for cultivating their latent powers, and we will develop here an industrial community, that can not only compete but will outstrip, in my opinion, the best efforts of Germany and her people. I hope that some means will be devised by which the provinces of this Dominion, on whom rests primarily the responsibility of this great matter, will become imbued with and awakened to their responsibilities, and to the duties which lie before them to give practical effect to a thorough system of technical education.
Mr. GEORGE W. KYTE (Richmond, N. S.): The importance of this question having been presented to the House on several occasions, I do not propose, at this late hour of the discussion, to enlarge upon the subject. I was, however, impressed with the observations just made by the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Glass). I think the ground he has taken is that until the Provincial Governments, to whose jurisdiction more particularly the question of education belongs, take the matter up and deal with it in a comprehensive and satisfactory manner, this Government ought not to be called upon to take any action. He further intimated that when that time comes this Government should be called upon to assist the provinces. Speaking for the province of Nova Scotia, I desire to say that the Government of that province has been the pioneer, I believe, on the subject of technical education in this Dominion. Some ten years ago the Government of Nova Scotia embarked on a very comprehensive and effective system of technical education. They built a technical college at Halifax at a coat of $100,000. It has the very best equipment from every point of view, and it is in charge of a competent and efficient staff of professors. The province of Nova Scotia, as you, Mr. Speaker, know well, is not by any means one of the largest and most opulent provinces of Canada. We are one of the smallest, both in area and in population, and we are also one of the smallest in respect of revenue. But the Government of Nova Scotia, realizing tHe need for a course of technical education for the young men employed in industrial pursuits in the province, felt that, notwithstanding the large
TMr. Glass.]
obligations, of one kind and another, were pressing upon them, those industrial interests ought not to be overlooked. As I have said, for that reason, the Government embarked ten years ago upon a system of technical education which has already borne excellent fruit. We are becoming a great industrial province, and advantage is being taken by many hundreds of young men of the courses which are available to them at that college. I think that the time has come for this Government to do something in the way of relieving the province of Nova Scotia of a portion of the burden involved in carrying on this important branch of its educational system. I was very pleased indeed to learn that my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Glass) took the ground that, where a province has already embarked upon a system of technical education, this Government should supplement its efforts by a grant. The right hon. the Prime Minister is perfectly familiar with the conditions as I have described them, and I sincerely nope that, if the Government is not prepared to enter into a comprehensive scheme of technical education throughout the whole Dominion of Canada, they will at least recognize the claims of Nova Scotia to some assistance, and at an early date make provision to assist by a grant technical education in that province.

Since the report to which the hon. member for Rouville's resolution refers was presented to this Parliament, this country has become engaged in a great war. A great statesman, in fact, great statesmen, have said that conditions will never be the same again after this war as they were before. The amount of money that will be involved in the payment of pensions alone, by reason of the war, will exceed per annum the amount which the report of the Commission on Technical Education recommended should be spent. I cannot therefore understand why my hon. friend urges this resolution at this time. If nothing will ever be the same again as it was before the war, if the annual charge upon our revenues is . constantly increasing by reason of the war, if we have to take care of pensions, which I regret to say are ever increasing, is it not quite apparent that the whole scheme and system of technical education will have to be reconsidered and revised in the light of the experience which we have derived during the last two years. Nothing is clearer, nothing is plainer, and therefore, I cannot quite understand why

my hon. friend from Rouville insists upon pressing a resolution which, if carried, will commit the Government of this country to giving effect to a report which was drafted in times of peace, which had regard to peace conditions, and which has not been in any way tinctured or changed or modified by reason of the war conditions with which we are confronted.
Might I make this observation, that I do not think this is either the time or the place in which to discuss this question. The whole social and economic condition of this country must change after the war. The large question of technical education is linked up inseparably with those social conditions, and with our system of colonization, and colonization in turn can only be developed in this country if we secure for those who settle within our boundaries better conditions than obtain in other countries. And better conditions surely mean that this state, as a state, both federal nad provincial, will be ' committed to the advancement of technical education.. I listened to the splendid observations of the hon. member for Rouville, to the observations of the Minister of Labour, and of my hon. friend beside me (Mr. Glass). I am not concerned about what somebody tells me is happening in Germany, in England, or in the United States; not a bit. But I am vitally concerned with the conditions that confront me in this country. The only value to Canadians of what takes place in Germany or in the United States is that is may serve as a guiding lamp by the aid of which we may follow the proper direction. What do I care about how Germany succeeded here or there? Germany did not have any country such as mine; she had no vast undeveloped natural resources such as we have; she had no country as large as the United States with a limited population, no such conditions as we have in Canada. There is no individual in Canada, who has given any thought to this matter, who has not the profound conviction that technical education is absolutely essential to the welfare of this state. That being so, all we can discuss is- the ways and means. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) can hardly be serious when he asks this Parliament to adopt a scheme which, as I have said, was prepared in times of peace, and which referred to no such conditions as those we are now confronted with. We are all agreed that the social and economic condition of this country must change after the war. Our colonization policy must be reshapen by the supreme effort of every man who calls himself a Canadian, so as to have a proper and efficient policy in the years to come, which will make the people of this country happier, more contented, and better settlers. Invited to come from other lands, they will find here the means to secure for themselves the proud position in the times of peace that they have -attained on the fields of war. That can never be done by talk. After the war, (the people of this country will not demand talk in Parliament. The men who come back from the front to this country will be sick of parliamentary talk. What they will demand is strong leadership, and if they do not get it from one party, they will get it from another; -and if they do not get it from the other they will get it from some middle party. They will demand leadership, initiative, and the carrying out of the reforms which have been suggested by this war. But this is not the time for us -to pledge ourselves. The men on both sides of politics who are supremely concerned with the welfare of the state should see to it that all the time we can give, and all the ability at our disposal, are devoted to an endeavour to shape a policy that will conform to the altered conditions brought about by the war. We must see that those who return from the battlefields, some strong, some wounded, -some maimed-those hundreds of thousands of men who have gone from our shores-will be admitted to a system of education which must be worked out harmoniously, not by appealing to the prejudices of this locality or of that, but by strong harmonious action on the part of the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments, to the end that the Canadian people may as successfully pursue the paths of peace as they have distinguished themselves in the times of war. For these reasons, I cannot understand why my hon. friend from Rouville presents his resohition at this time. I trust that -he -may reconsider the matter, and that he may feel constrained to withdraw his resolution under the circumstances, because there is no man within the sound of my Voice who is not as vitally interested in the matter as he is. All the people of this country realize that something must be done to prepare Canada for the great problems that confront her, but these can only be solved by revising and recasting our policies in the light of the great experience through which we have passed.
I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) -that we should postpone preparation for technical education until the war is over.
I did not say that. I said until such time as we were -able to revise and recast our plans in the light of the experience gained -since the report of the commission was -drafted.

I understood my hon. friend to mean that we should postpone preparation until such time ae we were financially capable of dealing with the mat-tier, or until the war was over. I quite agree with him that the expenses connected with the payment of pensions will be very great, no matter how careful we may be. At the same time, I think we should prepare now to assist, those men who are coming, and will come back from the front, by a system of technical education, or by what I would call industrial schools. Such a system would save this countrty a great deal of money in the end. We should get ready to place those men in industrial schools, so th-at they can learn to help themselves. A great many will not be able to return -to the trades which they followed before they went to the front, but they will be able to -learn other trades by which they could assist themselves very materially in maintaining themselves after the war is over I -am sure that al-1 of us would rather see them maintaining themselves than being -maintained entirely by the country. Therefore, I would urge that we cannot commence too soon. It takes -quite a long time to organize anything of this kind, because it is -a very larg-e question. But now is the time to get ready to organize, to receive those men when they come back, and that is saying nothing at all about the population generally being prepared to compete with other countries. As to what my hon. friend the Minister of Labour said as to the matter being under the jurisdiction of the province, nobody suggests that it is not. What is suggested is that the Dominion should work with the provinces, and I am sure that there is no province which would refuse to work amicably. with the Dominion in an effort- to carry out this worthy object.

Will my hon. friend tell us how, in view of the attitude of the provinces towards this question, he would propose to distribute the money? When the

recommendation of the commission that $3,350,000 should be distributed annually was communicated to them, they did not even reply, stating whether they approved of it or not, or whether they had any machinery with which to carry out the recommendation.

I cannot imagine that
there would be any difficulty in negotiating with the provinces. The probability is that the matter was allowed to drop, though I do not know -about that. I am not taking a party view of the matter. I cannot imagine that the Premier of any province would refuse to negotiate with the Dominion. As I have already said, it will take quite a long time to carry the negotiations through, and for that reason I urge that now is the time for the Dominion to get ready to work with the provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
We have had a very interesting and very instructive discussion on the important subject of technical education. First, we heard my h-on. friend from Rouville, who is at all times interesting in any speech which he delivers on an important question, and he was followed by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, who delivered one of the most interesting and most lucid speeches dealing with this question that, I fancy, has ever been delivered in this House. The question before us is one of great interest to the members of this House, and, I am sure, to the people of this country, and I desire that we should not have any misunderstanding upon it. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) that the question is liable to be misunderstood by some of the provinces in that they may regard any action we might take as interfering with their provincial rights under the British North America Act. If my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), had been present this afternoon and had listened to the Minister of Labour, he would have it made clear to him that the Government are undertaking in various forms to provide for the returned soldiers in the matter of education and everything that appertains to their welfare. The part that I do not wish to be misunderstood is this. My hon. friend from Rouville has moved a resolution asking this House to commit itself to the adoption of the recommendations of the report, as made by the Royal Commission on Technical Education a few years ago, in which they recommend that we

contribute $3,500,000 for ten years for technical education. As my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has well said, if conditions were normal, and if we had not to deal with war conditions, there would he some ground for the support which my hon. friend from Rouville has given to the recommendations of the Royal Commission. But I am sure that my hon. friend from Rouville does not himself believe at this moment that this House should accept the recommendations of that Commission and pledge itself to undertake to contribute $3,500,000 a year for the support of technical education. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve in addressing the House this evening, stated that an expenditure by this Government of $500,000, instead of $3,500,000, would be a sufficient contribution for the time being at all events, towards technical education. In view of the differences of opinion that appear to exist even in this House, and in view of the sensitive manner in which the question of education is considered by the various provinces, I think that my hon. friend from Rouville will see the force of my suggestion when I urge upon him that he should not press his resolution, and especially when I remind him that, as stated by my hon. friend the "Minister of Labour this afternoon, the Government recognizes the principle of assistance in the matter of technical education. We are giving the question to-day the most careful consideration, and under normal conditions we would be coming down to this House with a recommendation for a large sum to assist technical education in the various provinces. In view of this I trust that my hon. friend will not press his resolution but that he will accept the statement that the Minister of Labour has made to-day, and the assurance which I add, that this Government acknowledge the principle and that we will at the earliest possible moment lend such assistance as we can in the public interest to the furtherance of the cause of technical education in the provinces of Canada.

I have just prepared a short amendment to my motion which dovetails in with the happy remarks which have been made by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). I will read my amended resolution and I think it will meet the opinion of the House:
That in the opinion of this House measures should he taken at the earliest opportunity to promote, in co-operation with the provinces, technical education and manual training.
