The House resumed, from Monday, March 6, consideration of the proposed resolution of Mr. H. H. iStovens (Vancouver):
That, in the opinion of this House, at this time when the Empire is at war, the conservation of wealth and the resources of the Dominion and the promotion of the efficiency of our nation would be materially aided by the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale

of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes, and legislation for this purpose should be enacted forthwith.	*

What is the Alberta
scheme?

The Alberta scheme is legislation of the same character as the Macdonald Act, so called. It is a prohibitory measure that was initiated by virtue of a statute providing for direct legislation by which a petition was presented to the Legislature and a referendum then taken. The referendum was as to whether or not the Legislature should pass a prohibitory law; the .suggested prohibitory law being printed and circulated throughout the province before it was adopted.
Having regard to these results in the various provinces, we have to consider what our attitude should be as ia Parliament, representing not ofie province but all the people of the Dominion. I am not unaware of the argument that may be advanced against the exercise by this Parliament of any of its powers. There .are men who conscientiously 'believe that they should not be restricted in the use of alcoholic liquors as a beverage. I respect their convictions. IE there is one thing that the educational propaganda that has been carried on during the past twenty-five years has done more than any other, it is to teach men and women who have been engaged in temperance work to respect the profound and conscientious convictions of those who are opposed to pro-h'ibition. It is no longer regarded as useful in carrying on a propaganda for temperance to abuse a man who sells intoxicants; it used to be. A man who engages in the sale of intoxicants by the aid of a license has just as much right, as long as he obeys the law, to the protection of the law as any other man who carries on business under a license. The day when abuse was regarded as the one asset with which to conduct a propaganda of that kind has passed away, thanks, as I have said, to the education of our people with relation to the true matter at issue. Admitting, as I do, the right of every man to differ from me; admitting the right of men to believe conscientiously that they should not be restricted in the use of intoxicants; admitting the objection that most Anglo-Saxons have to the passing of sumptuary

laws, I purpose shortly to discuss this matter from the standpoint of a sumptuary law, from the standpoint of a police regulation, and from the standpoint of its social and economic effects.
Most men object to being told what they should eat and what they should drink. There is no man so bold in this House as to say that the liquor traffic should not be restricted and regulated. If, then, the traffic should be restricted and regulated, what is to determine the extent to which that regulation should be carried? What but the voice of democracy; what but the will of the people? Every man sitting within the sound of my voice this night knows that the price of our civilization is the surrender by each man of some of his individual liberties. The price of freedom is the exercise of self restraint and discipline. The price of liberty is the sacrifice of some of our personal rights, privileges, and advantages. The price of civilization is the exercise on the part of each of restraint and the surrender of some of his rights. So, with relation to what I shall eat and what I shall drink, I have to surrender something, because the system of Government under which I live is a system by which the voice and will of the people must determine what the laws shall be, and once democracy determines that I shall not have a drink of whisky, that moment I must sacrifice my right to	it. That is the
price of our civilization. We may not like it. There may be men who seriously object to it; there may be men who have conscientious convictions that such is unsound law. Nevertheless, the very founda- * tion of responsible representative institutions in this country is that the voice and will of democracy shall determine what is and what is not a sound sumptuary law. So far as personal liberty is concerned, there is nothing in that argument beyond what 1 have just said. The voice and will of the great majority of the people of this country determines what my personal rights shall be. .1 may not walk down the street unclothed, because the will of .society is that I shall not. I may not drink this or eat that because the will of society as expressed through the voice of the people has said, nay. But, Sir, there is a higheT ground; there is a ground the highest upon which I can conceive a man can base his reason for supporting a sumptuary law and enforcing a prohibitory law so far as liquor is concerned. It is the voice of Paul; it is
the voice of that great apostle of our common religion: " If by eating meat I make my brother to offend, I will eat no meat while the world stands." Upon that ground, it seems to me, we can base the soundest argument that can be made so far as the use of intoxicants as a beverage is concerned, because upon the third ground that I shall speak of presently we have ample reason for believing- nay, we must believe; we cannot help it- that the use of intoxicants is fraught with great disaster to the state, and the duty and the power of example necessitate our curtailing what might he our conception of personal liberty for the purpose of the advancement of the state as a whole.
Let us go a step further and deal with the second ground, that of police regulation. No man, within the sound of my voice tonight does not believe that the restriction and regulation of the liquor traffic is necessary from the police standpoint. Every man will at once concede that there may come a time when in the interests of efficient enforcement of police regulations, what was a restriction and regulation should become a prohibition. What determines that, mark you, must always be the voice of democracy. We have before us every day, whether we like it or not, examples of the misuse of intoxicants: poverty, suffering of the innocent, loss of labour, loss of wealth, both of the nation and the individual-all these things are everywhere visible to us.

The breaking up of
homes.
MR. BENNETT: I was going to mention in the next breath the sad domestic results .which follow: The innocent suffering, the children deprived of the support to which they should be entitled, the homes destroyed, the destruction of everything that goes to make for the national life of a country and the upbuilding of character, which is the greatest asset a country can possess. The social side of this evil involves the interference with those relations which characterize a great state, the domestic relations, the upbuilding of a sound ap* preciation and ideal of domestic life. On the economic side you have the waste that comes. I am not here to-night to measure that waste in dollars and cents. I am not here to-night to point out the great less that would ensue if we should pass prohibitory legislation, the loss of inland revenue and customs duties, which would

' amount to perhaps $20,000,000 a year. For all these things we would be amply compensated by the gain that would come owing to the added power and wealth, the savings of the people, by the labour that would not be interfered with or destroyed during the week, and by the comfort that would come to home and children, by the domestic happiness, by the lessened expense for police forces and the maintenence of our legal institutions-by all those things, as has been pointed out by a Lord Chief Justice in England, that would become unnecessary but for the habits of the people which have grown up through long years of use, until the people have come to regard liberty as a license to carry on these habits in perpetuity. Sometimes I thank Heaven that in a new country like this we have the example of an older country to guide us, so that we may at least profit by the mistakes that have been made by them, and: that in a new land such as this, where we have a small population, we are far away and ahead of those, who, by reason of their old country amd their old institutions and old habits, have not been able, by reason of vested interests and other considerations, to shake off the shackles that have bound them to particular habits of customs. Enough as to that. I think the case for interference by legislation is sufficient.
Let us now come at once to the unit of our efforts, namely the province. I have already referred to what has been done in the various provinces. Let me ask this question of the House, which seems to me after all, the crux of this whole isisue: Within what'area and to what extent shall the will of the majority prevail over the will of the minority with respect to the tastes and appetites of the people? Let me take a concrete case. The city of Montreal, perhaps the island of Montreal has, let me say, one-tenth of the population of Canada. Would it be sound statesmanship to say that the will of the rest of the people of Canada, constituting a majority of the various provinces, should prevail over the will of that minority? Or would it be sounder statecraft to say that the will of the majority in the province in which that island is should prevail over the minority within that island? That is a concrete case. Would it be fair or right to say that the will of the majority in the other eight provinces should prevail over the will of the majority in the province of British Columbia? That is a majority in so far as that province is

concerned. That is, if there be in British Columbia a majority against prohibition, would you look for a faithful enforcement of the law if you said that the will of the majority in the other eight provinces should prevail over the will of the majority in the province of British Columbia? Or would you .say that sound principle and the dictates of common sense and reason alike tell you, that if you desire to have a sound prohibition law you must always make your province the unit, so that, by the process of education to which I have referred,
' the will of the majority in that province should always determine what should be the legislation of that province? That is the problem, what should be the unit of area, as a gentleman said to me yesterday, of home rule with relation to the liquor traffic? Which is a very excellent and fair way to put it. Let us look at that in all its features. You have the province of Prince Edward Island, you have Nova Scotia, you have New Brunswick, and you have Ontario, we will say; and within the limits and boundaries of these provinces they have fairly well made up their minds, by reasonable majorities, that they will have prohibitory legislation. We will say that the province of Quebec, by a majority, thinks otherwise. Do you think you will have an efficient administration of the law if you pass a law common to all those provinces by which you propose to coerce the opinion of Quebec by virtue of a majority outside of and beyond the boundary of that province? That is the problem. That is the position you have to think about. Would any hon. gentleman in this Chamber say that be believes a Dominion wide prohibitory law passed by this Parliament to-day would be efficient and sound legislation unless it was backed by an enlightened and educated public opinion? No, he would not. Then, if he will not say that, I go a step further and ask him the next question:	Does he say that the will
of the province of Alberta would be effective in coercing the will of the people in British Columbia? Surely he will say no to that. Would he say that the combined opinion of the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, used to overcome the views of the majority in the opposite direction from the province of British Columbia, would make efficient legislation? There is behind it in British Columbia, you see, no efficient public opinion, no enlightened public opinion, and, by calling upon the public opinion from two outside units

or areas, you ask that combined public opinion, as representing a majority in those provinces, to overcome and thwart and destroy the will of the democracy in the province to the west. Suppose you come to .the East once more, to reiterate this argument which is the basis of it all, it seems to me. Is it sound to say that the will of a majority representing large numbers in the province of Ontario shall overcome the convictions and conscientious views in the opposite direction of the province of Quebec? Do you think you would have sound legislation? Do you think you could efficiently enforce it? Then you come to the other provinces and apply the same principle. I think, therefore, without endeavouring to waste the time of the House by a lengthy argument, you must conclude with me that the unit within which you can hope to make efficient laws, backed up by a sound and enlightened public opinion must be the physical boundaries of the province in the first instance. But from a constitutional standpoint, those provinces enforcing merely prohibitory laws, so long as they are part of this Dominion, and interprovincial trade is freely carried on, cannot hope to make their laws efficient except within their own borders. They cannot stop the importation into one province of liquor from other provinces. The province of Prince Edward Island, in the extreme east, having determined, as it has, by a majority substantial in number, that it will prohibit the use of intoxicants as a beverage, cannot, under our constitution, restrict or restrain the importation of liquor from the province of Nova Scotia or the province of New Brunswick or the province of Quebec. The very essence of our constitution is freedom in interprovincial trade. What happens? The limited powers of the Legislature precluding the possibility of their passing the necessary statute to prohibit importation, they find that their efforts, the will of the people, the will of the democracy within that province, is thwarted by reason of their being unable to express themselves in legislative form. I come to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and I find that the same conditions prevail. I come to Manitoba and I find the same conditions. I come to Alberta and I find the same conditions. Then it is with me a simple problem: What legislation, backed by an efficient public opinion representing the educated and enlightened views of the
democracy, shall Ibe passed by this Parliament which will enable the will of the democracy within the province to be made effective. That is the question I have to ask myself, and I am not content to approach that problem or that question in the light of visionary philosophy. I desire to approach it from the standpoint of sound, political, concrete necessity. And what legislation do I ask? My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island has suggested the amendment of the British North America Act. Another gentleman has suggested the widening of the constitutional power of the provinces in another way. I cannot agree to this, so long as I find within the four corners of the present constitution, methods and means whereby I can make effective the views I hold. I find that when the Canada Temperance Act was passed it went to the Privy Council to determine whether or not it was competent for this Parliament to pass that Act or whether or not it trenched upon and interfered with the exclusive rights of the provinces? I do not desire to make to this tribunal a legal argument, but there are a few elementary propositions which it seems to me may be fairly stated, and which the layman may have no difficulty in understanding. Under the provisions of our British, North America Act matters of a national concern were entrusted to this Parliament. We were given the power to regulate trade and commerce, and the Privy Council has said that means trade and commerce in the large and wide sense of the term, not only trade, buit trade and commerce as these matters affect the welfare of the nation as a whole. That is under subsection 2 of section 91 of the British North America Act, which section defines, in general terms, the powers that may be exercised by this Parliament, while section 92 defines the powers that may be exercised by Provincial Legislatures. The powers among others that may foe exercised by Provincial Legislatures are with respect to the raising of revenue by licenses, with respect to property and civil rights, and with respect generally to matters of a local character. Now, if we keep in mind trie** principles, in the light of the interpretation of that Act by the Privy Council, we [DOT] have evolved for us certain well fixed rules which I shall not take the trouble to state at length, but some of which I shall endeavour to present briefly to the House.
The case of Russell v. the Queen, which went to the Privy Council, involved an

interpretation of the Canada Temperance Act which came into force after being voted upon by a majority of the people of any county or municipality. That Act was prohibitory in its character; it was of Dominion-wide application, and it was contended before the Privy Council that it was an interference with the property and civil rights within the province of New Brunswick. But the Privy 'Council determined that, inasmuch as it was a statute dealing with a condition throughout the Dominion as a whole, and for the peace, order and good government of Canada, it was within the competency of this Parliament to pass it.
There followed upon that Act a local option Act from the province of Ontario, and the case Hodge v. the Queen, involved the determination of the constitutionality of a statute passed by the Legislature of Ontario in 1877, I think. That statute created licensing districts, gave local option in certain communities, and was in fact the basis on which the Ontario License Act was founded. That Act was held to be within the competence of the Legislature of Ontario. It was contended with great force that the legislatures of the provinces did not exercise plenary powers, that they only exercised subordinate powers, and had not the same free rights of legislation as appertain to a free Parliament. The Privy Council gave no force or effect to the contention. The Privy Council dealt with the matter at a later date, and 1 desire to quote from that decision 'because it puts the matter much more clearly than I possibly could. It says:
The object of the Act was neither to weld the provinces into one, nor to subordinate provincial governments to a central authority, but to create a federal government in which they should all be represented, entrusted with the exclusive administration of affairs in which they had a common interest, each province retaining its independence and autonomy. That object was accomplished by distributing between the Dominion and the provinces all powers, executive and legislative, and all public property and revenues, which had previously belonged to the provinces, so that the Dominion Government should be vested with such of these powers, property, and revenues as were necessary for the due performance of its constitutional functions, and that the remainder should he retained by the provinces for the purposes of provincial government. But, in so far as regards those matters, which, by section 92, are specially reserved for provincial legislation, the legislation of each province continues to he free from the control of the Dominion and as supreme as it was before the passing of the Act. In Hodge vs. the Queen, 9 AC., 117, Lord Fitzgerald, delivering the opinion of this hoard, said: "When the British

North America Act enacted that there should be a legislature for Ontario, and that its Legislative Assembly should have exclusive authority to make laws for the province and for provincial purposes in relation to the matters enumerated in section 92, it conferred powers not in any sense to be exercised by delegation from or as agents of the Imperial Parliament, hut authority as plenary and as ample within the limits prescribed by section 92 as the Imperial Parliament in the plentitude of its power possessed and could bestow. Within these limits of subject and area, the local legislature is supreme, and has the same authority as the Imperial Parliament, or the Parliament of the Dominion." The Act places the constitutions of all provinces within the Dominion on the same level, and what is true with respect to the legislature of Ontario has equal application to the legislature of New Brunswick.
That being so, and property and civil
rights being one of the subject matters committed exclusively to the provinces, it follows that it was given entirely to the provinces to determine what property a man should have in anything even if it should be a glass of intoxicating liquor. It is competent for the Legislature of the province of Manitoba or of Ontario to determine whether, or not, a man shall have in his possession a single drop of intoxicants. It is competent for the Legislature of Ontario to declare that a man shall not have property in a single pint or gill of intoxicants within the area of that province, because legislation affecting property and civil rights, and all that appertain to these two terms, are exclusively within the power of the provincial legislature.
After the cake of Hodge v. the Queen, there followed in 1890 the case from Ontario known as the Prohibition case, in which certain questions were submitted to the court for the purpose of determining what rights the province had with relation to the manufacture and importation of intoxicating liquors. The case was decided in 1895. The questions were very numerous and the , Privy Council did not answer them all contenting itself with answering a few and leaving the guiding principles for the determination of the balance. The first question wa.s:
Has .a provincial legislature jurisdiction to prohibit the sale within the province of spirituous, fermented, or other intoxicating liquors?
The answer is " Yes. " The next question was:
Or has the legislature such jurisdiction regarding such portions of the province as to which the Canada Temperance Act is not in operation?
The answer is " Yes. "

Has a provincial legislature jurisdiction to prohibit the manufacture of such liquors within the province.
That is a vital question and the answer to it I should like to read in the terms of the Privy Council judgment. The answer was this:
In the absence of conflicting legislation by the Parliament of Canada, their Lordships are of opinion that the provincial legislatures would have jurisdiction to that effect if it were shown that the manufacture was carried on under such circumstances and conditions as to make its prohibition a. merely local matter in the province.
In other words, if, in the city of Edmonton, there is a brewery making beer, all of which is sold entirely within the province, it is competent for the Provincial Legislature to pass a Bill prohibiting the manufacture of beer by that brewery. But if, on the other Rand, a brewery carried on an interprovincial trade and an export business the circumstances are such that the Provincial Legislature could not prohibit the manufacture of beer in that brewery. The next question was this:
Has a provincial legislature jurisdiction to prohibit the importation of such liquors into the province?
The answer is this:
Their Lordships answer this question in the negative. It appears to them that the exercise by the provincial legislature of such jurisdiction in the wide and general terms in which it is expressed, would probably trench upon the exclusive authority of the Dominion parliament.
The other questions deal with matters that I need not allude to at the present time, the two questions that I particularly desire to direct the attention of the House to being those concerned with the manufacture and .importation of liquor. If then it is competent, as the Privy Council has said it is, for a provincial legislature to pass the necessary legislation to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicants within the limits of the province for the purpose of undertaking to supply merely the local needs, it follows that that is all that is necessary to effect prohibition within the province if you supplement it with the unquestioned power of the legislature to prohibit the sale within the province. In other words, a brewery or a distillery that carries on business and sells its product outside of the province may carry on that business. But no distillery, or brewery, can manufacture and sell within the province because the provincial legislature can
prohibit such sale. A brewery or distillery which carries on business for purely local consumption can be prohibited by the province.
Does the hon. gentleman know of any such brewery in Canada?
Yes, there are breweries in my part of the country which sell their products only within the province.
If they sell one gallon outside of the province that would override the Act?

They could carry on an interprovincdal business. But that must be the character of their business. It does not mean the sale of a single gallon. I would sooner accept the answer of the Privy Council than my own opinion; and that is that if the character of the business was purely local and provincial they would have the power to prohibit; otherwise they would be within my understanding of the answer of the Privy Council.

It would be a very precarious sort of legislation, would not my hon. friend admit, because the moment any quantity, or shipment of a commercial character, went from the province, the legislation would not stand the test any longer.

That might well be, but that is not a practical question for the simple reason that if the sale is forbidden within the province, the province has the absolute and sole power over it. A little brewery that only supplies one province does not make any difference because the sale of its product is within the province and the province has the power to prohibit. Now, I am going to express an opinion that may not meet with the approval of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House or, for that matter, of hon. gentlemen sitting beside me. I do not believe it is my duty as a Canadian to undertake to legislate for the Argentine Republic, or England, or the United States of America, and if they want to buy beer or whisky I am not going to arrogate to myself the right to determine whether they shall or shall not drink it. I trust that experience has taught me the lesson that the less I have to do with other people's business, especially when they live outside of my own country, the better it is for me and for them. The principle is this: the manufacture of spirits may be carried on in Canada provided it is for export only, and I

am not concerned about it because it may well be that there are people who do not look upon the use of .spirituous liquor as a beverage as we do, who have not been educated as we have,,and I do not propose to undertake the education of people in other countries in regard to the principles of temperance. It is perfectly clear that while the province cannot deal with the manufacture or interprovincial trade or export, there is no reason why the Canadian people should not manufacture anything that other people want to buy. . I have not reached that stage in regard to the temperance question where I am prepared to say: You cannot manufacture or export whiskey from Canada if other people want to use it. I desire to be perfectly frank about this and I have no apologies to offer for expressing my opinion in a perfectly frank manner on this point.

It is said in the newspapers that the Attorney General of Manitoba has made the statement that legislation such as is proposed by the Bill submitted by the Minister of Justice is ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada according to section 121 of the British North America Act. Was the hon. gentleman's attention called to that?

I will read that section:
All articles of the growth, produce or manufacture of any one of the provinces shall, from and after the Union, be admitted free into each of the other provinces.
I have a moat proper respect for any gentleman who calls himself attorney general of any of the provinces of Canada, but I do not think that there is a layman in any province who would say that that section has anything to do with out Bill. This is a matter of history. Any man who has read the Confederation debates at Quebec, will remember that before the British North America Act was passed, between the provinces there were duties and in fact, the province of New Brunswick found it rather difficult to give up certain payments which it received in relation to timber, and there was a little money paid to them in connection with that matter. We had tariffs between the provinces and it was to make it clear that in this federal union there should be freedom of interprovincial trade, the same as in the United States a constitutional provision was introduced for freedom of interstate commerce, that we have that section. The section is so clear that I think my hon.

friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) will see that it must have no bearing on this Bill. I will read it again:
All articles of the growth, produce or manufacture of any one of the provinces shall, from and after the Union, be admitted free into each of the other provinces.
The legislation that I am going to speak about just now does not in any way curtail freedom, but it makes it an offence to do certain things. That is all. For instance, there are acts bearing on this point and I will give an illustration that occurs to me.
Will the hon. gentleman say that a certain thing is free when it is an offence to do it?

Yes, .under certain conditions.
Mr. MARCH.: Free in that case means free from customs duties.

Absolutely; free from
any impost of the character or nature of customs. I want to give an illustration because as I am dealing with the matter I might as well make it complete. Hon. gentlemen will remember the legislation passed some years ago in connection with the killing of fur-bearing animals, making it an offence to carry the furs of such animals from one country, or one province, to another. You may,, under certain conditions, apprehend a man who kills and takes furs notwithstanding the fact that he may have done it in another province.
Trade has nothing to do with the creation of an offence of another character altogether?

This deals with trade
and the other deals with the exercise of criminal law, and the criminal law may not he susceptible of universal application. You may have some sections which are limited in their application to one particular part of the country. But there is another point that occurs to me just now and it answers that conclusively. In the year 1908 this Parliament passed exactly the same section as this Bill contains mutatis mutandis in relation to the Canada Temperance Act We have gone a little further. [DOT] We enacted in 1908, in this Parliament, that if, in a Scott Act county, there was an importation from a non-Scott Act county, that that should be an offence. That law has been on the statute-book eight years, and nobody has questioned the constitutionality

of it. I am afraid the Attorney-General for Manitoba has not been correctly reported-	-
It was in the papers.
-'because I know the Hon. Mr. Hudson and I have a high regard for him; his ability is admitted- on all hands.
In some directions.

In some directions, we will say, because there may be different view points, and there are various shades of ability. I say that either he must have been incorrectly reported, or he is not conversant with the character of our legislation.
The last word of the Privy Council as to the powers of a province was given on the constitutionality of the Macdonald Act, and while I do not desire to trespass upon the time of the House, possibly you would not mind, Mr. Speaker, if I made a reference to that decision, because it is a matter of more than passing interest. The case was brought before the Privy Council in England in 1901, and the judgment was delivered by Lord Macnaghten, from which I quote:
In July, 1900, an Act was passed by the legislature of Manitoba for the suppression of the liquor traffic in that province. The Act, which is known by its short title of "The Liquor Act, " was to have come into operation on June 1, 1901. Before that date, on a reference under clause 28 of the Revised Statutes of Manitoba, the Court of King's Bench pronounced the Whole Act to be unconstitutional. From this decision the present appeal has been brought.
Although the questions submitted to the Court of King's Bench by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, were eleven in number, the only one considered in the court below, and the only one argued before this board, was the first:	"Had the
Legislative Assembly of Manitoba jurisdiction to enact the Liquor Act, and if not, in what particular or respect has it exceeded its power?" To this the answer given was, "It exceeded its powers in enacting the Liquor Act as a whole." The other questions are either of an academical character or such as are material only in the event of the Act being declared partially and not wholly unconstitutional. No answer that could be given to any of those questions would be of any practical value. Their lordships, therefore, will confine their attention to the subject to which the judgment of the Court of King's Bench and the arguments at the bar were addressed.
The question at issue depends on the meaning and effect of those sections in the British North America Act, 1867, which provide for the distribution of legislative powers between the Dominion and the provinces. The subject has been discussed before this board very frequently and very fully. Mindful of advice often
quoted (1), but not, perhaps, always followed, their lordships do not propose to travel beyond the particular case before them.
The drink question, to use a common expression which is convenient, if not altogether accurate, is not to be found specifically mentioned either in the classes of subjects enumerated in section 91 and assigned to the legislature of the Dominion, or in those enumerated in section 92 and thereby appropriated to provincial legislatures. The omission was probably not accidental. The result has been somewhat remarkable. On the one hand, according to Russell vs. Reg. (2) it is competent for the Dominion Legislature to pass an Act for the suppression of intemperance applicable to all parts of the Dominion, and when duly brought into operation in any particular district deriving its efficacy from the general authority vested in the Dominion Parliament to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada. On the other hand, according to the decision in Attorney General for Ontario vs. Attorney General for the Dominion (3) it is not incompetent for a provincial legislature to pass a measure for the repression, or even for the total abolition, of the liquor traffic within the province, provided the subject is dealt with as a matter "of a merely local nature" in the province, and the Act itself is not repugnant to any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
In delivering the judgment of this board in the case of Attorney General for Ontario vs. Attorney General for the Dominion (1) Lord Watson expressed a decided opinion that provincial legislation for the suppression of the liquor traffic could not be supported under either No. 8 or No. 9 of section 92.
*
He added that it was not necessary for the purpose of that appeal to determine whether such legislation was authorized by the one oi by the other of these heads. Although this particular question was thus left apparently undecided, a careful perusal of the judgment leads to the conclusion that, in the opinion of the board, the case fell under No. 16 rather than under No. 13. And that seems to their lordships to be the better opinion. In legislating for the suppression of the liquor traffic the object in view is fcthe abatement or prevention of a local evil, rather than the regulation of property and civil rights-though, of course, no such legislation can be carried into effect without interfering more or less with "property and civil rights in the province." Indeed, if the case is to be regarded as dealing with matters within the class of subjects enumerated in No. 13, it might be questionable whether the Dominion Legislature could have authority to interfere with the exclusive jurisdiction of the province in the matter.
The controversy, therefore, seems to be narrowed to this one point: Is the subject of "The Liquor Act" a matter "of a merely local nature in the province" of Manitoba, and does the Liquor Act deal with it as such?

A province does not go further because it has no power to go further. The legislation introduced by the Minister of Justice does not add anything of value, because the province of Ontario cannot prohibit a person in Ontario from importing liquor from another province for his own use. The Macdonald Act cited by the hon. gentleman shows that it has no such intention. The province of Ontario does not prohibit the importation of liquor because it has not power to do so.
I am sorry my hon. friend has not followed the reasoning of the Privy Council. It is competent for a Legislature to pass an Act saying that possession of intoxicating liquors shall be an offence.
An offence against a provincial statute?

The Legislature can say that it shall be an offence to have liquor in one's possession. If that be so, if you buy it in the province, there is a sale and the action is punishable by provincial law; but if you bring .it in and get it into your possession by importation, the carrier and the importer and the shipper are liable under this legislation. Have I made myself clear?

No. If under the Dominion Act you have the right to import liquor from another province or another country, the province cannot prevent that, unless you import the liquor for the purpose of sale or otherwise to violate the law passed by the province.

My hon. friend has quite grasped the principle; it is in the application that we are at variance. This law will say that, wherever a province has, in the exercise of its undoubted legislative power, declared, for example, that the possession of a bottle of whiskey shall be an offence against the statute, then if a person buy's a bottle of whisky, he has committed

an offence because there has been a sale within the province. If he brings a bottle of whisky in from outside and gets it into his possession, he is guilty of an offence against this statute beoause the importation) made possession possible, which is an offence under the provincial statute. I trust my hon. friend has followed me.
I follow you, but no province has passed such legislation.

Yes, but the fact that a province has not exercised the power which the Privy Council says it may exercise is not the foundation of a good argument against the enactment of legislation which a province has the power to enact. On the contrary, it is a good reason why the people, with their eyes wide open, knowing fully the circumstances under which they enact their laws, should know that they have ancillary to their own statute, .supplementary to the powers conferred upon them by the British North America Act, the power contained in the legislation we are now about to pass whereby it is an offence to bring liquor into a province which has passed legislation prohibiting its citizens having liquor in their possession.

Under the Ontario measure, a person would have the right to buy from a retail druggist on a medical prescription six ounces of liquor. If a greater quantity than six ounces was found in his possession, would my hon. friend maintain that he was violating the law, or that it might be prima facie evidence that he had it for sale?

That would depend upon the terms of the provincial statute. The provincial statute would have to state that possession of more than six ounces of liquor was prima facie evidence of having it for sale.
If the statute said so, would my hon. friend say that it would be a constitutional offence?

If the statute said so, it certainly would be. I do not, however, know what the details of the statute may be. It occurs to me that we should endeavour to enact effective legislation applicable throughout this Dominion that may supplement the legislation of any province. I have conceded the importance of the issue, the magnitude of the question, the necessity for legislation. I have endeavoured to point out how regulation and
restriction have been followed by prohibition passed by various provinces, and I have endeavoured, I trust with some degree of success, to indicate that the unit or area should be the province. Let me point out that there has been standing on the statute. book of the Dominion for thirty-
11 p.m. eight years, a law passed by this Parliament, that would have made possible a Dominion-wide prohibition, and yet it has not been taken advantage of. If the Canada Temperance Act, were brought into force in every county and municipality of the Dominion, you would have Dominion-wide prohibition. No effort, however, has been made to do that. In my view, this Parliament, unless and until there is unequivocal evidence that behind us is an enlightened and educated body of public opinion
How is that to be ascertained otherwise than from the facts we now have?
It would be ascertained by the action of the provinces.
And is the hon. gentleman not satisfied with the overwhelming majorities in the provinces in favour of prohibition?

I am not satisfied that there exists in this Dominion such a body of enlightened public opinion as will make and enforce a national prohibition law, and the reasons I have plainly given; but I am satisfied that, exercising the powers given to them within the ample scope of their authority under the constitution, the various legislatures, exercising their powers a little to-day, a little more to-morrow, until they have exercised the full powers given to them under the constitution, supplemented and implemented by the legislation which will be placed upon the statute-books of this country by this Parliament can insure prohibition within an area provincial in its boundaries, and behind that legislation it will have an enlightened and educated body of public opinion which will make it efficient.

I presume that my hon. friend speaks of a provincial area. Does he think that the Bill which has been introduced by the Minister of Justice to supplement any local legislation will also protect the enforcement of a provincial law as regards a lesser area? Let us take, for instance, the province of Quebec. Suppose that the province does not adopt prohibition

within its boundaries, but that many municipalities adopt prohibitory measures, would the legislation introduced by the Minister of Justice apply as well to those lesser areas as to the larger area, the provincial area?

I can only say that the language of the statute seems to contemplate that case. It says:
Any 'person who by himself, his clerk, servant or agent, shall send, ship, take, bring or carry to or into any province, from or out of any other province, or import into any province.
Of course, it would have to come from another 'province to meet that particular point. If it does not come from another province, but from the outside, this legislation is designed to meet that case. The Canada Temperance Act does meet the case, and if the importation came from a non-Scott area into a Scott Act area, then the provisions of the Canada Temperance Act Amendment of 1908 would apply. In view of all these facts to which I have directed the attention of the House. I beg to move the following amendment-

Before the hon. gentleman moves his amendment I would suggest to him that he has omitted entirely to deal with the main purpose of the resolution now before the House-that it should be adopted as an economic measure during the period of the war. Will he dwell on that aspect of the ease?

In Quebec 916 municipalities are dry at the present time. Any .prohibition law enacted by the legislature would apply only to those municipalities
which have not yet taken action.

The last observation
made by the hon. member for Bonaventure enforces more strongly thpn I can the argument that I was endeavouring to make If the 916 municipalities in the province of Quebec have not seen fit through their

legislature to impose their will upon the people of the city of Montreal, why should a. majority made up of the residents of, we will say, Alberta and Saskatchewan impose their will upon the people of that city?
You cannot prevent importation from the province of Ontario into Montreal by provincial legislation.

The moment the province passes a prohibitory law, then, by virtue of this legislation, importations into Montreal in contravention of that provincial measure of Quebec would be prohibited. I thank my hon. friend for his questions; they have directed my attention to points that I had overlooked.
I desire to move, seconded by Mr. Davidson, of Annapolis:
That all the words in the proposed resolution after the word " that " he struck out and the following substituted instead thereof:
This House recognizes the great advance made during the past twenty years in the several provinces of Canada through the enactment of laws for promoting temperance and for prohibiting or restricting the liquor traffic.
That the restriction and regulation of the liquor traffic cannot be efficiently accomplished except through public opinion fully supporting enactments passed for that purpose.
That as public opinion varies in the several provinces, it is desirable that such enactments depending for their efficient enforcement upon public opinion should in the first instance be determined by the respective legislatures of the several provinces.
That up to the full measure of provincial jurisdiction the subject should in the first instance be dealt with by the respective provincial legislatures.
That this Parliament should at the present session enact legislation to prohibit the transportation or importation of intoxicating liquor into any province for any use or purpose which is or may be forbidden by the law of such province.
I am not prepared at once to strive to make the reform which the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) contemplates. I have no doubt but that in the fulness of time such legislation as it contemplates ma-y be enacted by this Parliament. But as we pass the milestones that indicate the progress that the temperance movement has made, it must not (be forgotten that those milestones have not been passed in long strides. They indicate slow and weary steps that have been taken by those who have always had in mind the ultimate end-reform in the use of liquors as intoxicants, and the ultimate prohibition of their use as a beverage. Reforms will never be accomplished by too drastic measures. As I read history, great reforms have been accomplished by slow degrees,

by a step to-day and a step to-morrow, ever moving forward, so that where the vanguard camped to-day the rearguard may march to-morrow. It has always been so; it always will be so. The great reforms of Shaftsbury, of Romilly, of Howard, of Plimsoll, were brought about by a steady forward movement, keeping the goal ever in view, being content with a little here and a little there, to the end that there might be behind all legislation that strong and vigorous and educated public opinion without which legislation must fail. Unless we have behind us the sentiment of an aroused and educated public opinion that will decree that what we place on the statute-books must be enforced, then we had better have no legislation at all; because you bring your institutions into contempt and you cheapen the Parliament 'of your country in the eyes of the world if you pass legislation which you cannot or do not enforce. That is the view that I have, and that is the reason why, speaking as a life long abstainer, I think that the step we take if we pass this legislation submitted by the Minister of Justice, will be a step forward, and that it will maTk a milestone in the progress of temperance legislation such as will not be found in the statute-books of any country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, with the very able and very eloquent remarks that have just been made by the hon. member for Calgary, I very heartily concur, and it is with the greatest pleasure I rise to second the amendment which he has moved. As long ago as the year 1905, in a political campaign in my own constituency, I outlined my position on this very important question to be in favour of the different provincial legislatures going to the full extent of their constitutional powers in restriction of the liquor traffic, and in the passage of a Federal Act which would protect the various provinces from interference from outside. For the last ten years the opposition in the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia, with varying degrees of success, have advocated this policy, and it is with the greatest possible satisfaction to-night that I realize that this reform has now found so eloquent and so influential a champion as the hon. member for Calgary, and, most of all am I pleased that these propositions stand so excellent an opportunity at the present time of being crystallized into legislation.
The provisions of the amendment appear to me as to be so very reasonable that I do not think they require argument in order to be received favourably by this House. Particularly after tne exceedingly able and eloquent plea which has been presented by the mover of this amendment, I think very few words are required from me, and I do not propose to weary the House at any very great length on this occasion.
It strikes me that the severe and dam-aging arraignment of the evils of the liquor traffic which has been made by the mover (Mr. H. H. Stevens) and by the seconder (Hon. Charles Mareil) of this resolution, as well as by the various speakers who have spoken in its support, will find pretty general agreement in this House and throughout this country. The evils of the liquor traffic are so inherent that to-day they are appreciated both by the user and by the non-user of alcoholic liquors. But this was not always so. It has taken a long time for this evil to be viewed in its proper light. The role which alcohol has played in the human drama has been the role of the gay deceiver. When distilled liquor was first discovered it was welcomed as the elixir of life, and a remedy so exceedingly agreeable in its immediate effects naturally became very popular. It was pre- . ferred as a remedy to Sir Walter Raleigh's sharp instrument which cured all diseases in sickness and a very agreeable companion in health, the true aspect of this evil was not at first recognized. The people did not see the evil in its ugly nakedness as the most persistent enemy of mankind. But that time has at length come, and I think both the users and the non-users of intoxicating liquors to-day realize that the traffic is a curse'. Of course I am free to admit that it is possible to engage in the use of intoxicating liquor with very slight, if any, injurious effects; and sometimes it may be that the magnanimity of the . individual who does not use liquor and who' thinks that, for the benefit of the community as a whole, the use of it should be abolished, may be somewhat open to question. The American humorist was willing to sacrifice all his wifeh relations on the altar of his country. But the teetotaller to-day who favours, in the interests of the war, sacrificing his neighbour's habits and luxuries', may be regarded as possessing very much the same sort of heroism. Yet, as I said before, the economic evil of the liquor traffic is so great and its moral effect, so deleterious, that there is scarcely any

one in Canada so bound to this evil at the present time that he would not favour, if it were possible, its absolute eradication, its absolute destruction, root and branch. As I understand, the only extensive opposition that comes to the measure is that of people who think that such provisions may not be effective. If we could point with certainty to a law which would forever remove this evil from our midst, I think there is no one who would not uphold such a measure, andil believe that the principle outlined in the amendment which has just been made by my iron, friend will go a long way towards this conclusion.	.
I suppose that in no part of the world have greater strides been made towards the enactment of prohibitory temperance legislation than on the continent of North America; and yet I fancy that the legislative temperance reformer in the North American continent has encountered greater legislative obstacles than in any other part of the world. Both the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada are governed by a federal system. The federal system of government, while possessing many advantages, possesses many disadvantages as well. It necessitates a division of power, a division of legislative authority between the central or federal parliament and the state or provincial parliament. That division of authority has inevitably led to overlapping and uncertainty of legislation; but perhaps in no realm of legislative enactment has this obstacle been more apparent than in the enactment of temperance legislation. The temperance legislative reformer in the United States went to the various state legislatures for power to regulate this evil. By the constitution of the United States powers which are not expressly assigned to the Federal Congress lie in the various state ;legislatures. Consequently the legislative temperance reformer in the United States as a rule sought the instrumentality of the state legislatures in the effort to suppress this traffic. But he had not gone far before he encountered a constitutional obstruction. When the various state legislatures proceeded to prohibit or license the sale of liquors imported from foreign countries and from other states, they encountered a constitutional' difficulty, because the constitution of the United States provides that commerce, both interstate and foreign, shall be dealt with by the Federal Congress, .and by the Federal Congress alone. Thus when 
the various states attempted to decrease or restrict the use of liquor imported from abroad, they were met with the Objection that this was beyond their powers, that this was ultra vires; and consequently, in 1890, the Wilson Act was passed through the American Congress iin order to rectify this condition of affairs. The Wilson Act provided and declared that intoxicating liquors shall, upon arrival in a state, be subject to the operation of the police powers of the state. That was supplementary Federal legislation very much in line with the proposal made by my hon. friend, but that law did not go far enough to be effective. That law did not make it an offence to send into a state under prohibition, liquor from another state or from a foreign country; and as" a consequence the prohibition Acts passed by the various states of the American Union are only half measures, that permit of liquor being imported from other countries and from other states.
In the Dominion of Canada the temperance legislative reformers sought, I believe, in the first instance, principally the instrumentality of the Dominion or Federal Parliament, under the powers given by the British North America Act to the Federal Parliament to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada; and from Confederation up to the year 1900 this Parliament, was continually assailed by the temperance reformer with a request for prohibitory legislation. Under this power and in compliance with requests made by the temperance people, the Canada Temperance Act and other legislation was passed. As outlined by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), a constitutional war raged on this question from 1867 until 1890, and the Privy Council on various occasions pronounced upon the question. But the matter was really not effectively settled until the year 1900. In the year 1900 the Provincial Legislature of Manitoba, upder the premiership of the Hon.Hugh John Macdonald, passed 'a very drastic and very complete prohibitory law, a law which at the tifne oi its enactment was thought by constitutional authorities in Canada to be beyond the powers of the Manitoba Legislature. The matter was taken to the Privy Council and the Privy Council decided that the law was not ultra vires, and by so doing decided that the power of the various Provincial Legislatures to deal with this question was veTy extensive and very complete. From that time the advocate of

legislative prohibition in Canada largely deserted this House and devoted his energies principally to the Provincial Legislatures. I know the statement has been made that it was not the decision upon the Macdonald Act that influenced the temperance advocates in changing their policy. I know it. has been said that the Dominion Temperance Alliance, for instance, officered by Liberals, were influenced somewhat by the change of Government in the Dominion in 1896, and by the change of Government in the province of Ontario in 1900, that those people were not so zealous in coming to the Dominion with embarrassing requests after the change of Government in 1896, and showed a greater zeal in going to the Provincial Legislature in Ontario after the change of Government there in 1900. But I do not think that that is a fair statement. I think the temperance advocates in Canada saw from the decision of the Privy Council that the. Provincial Legislatures were the places to which they should go, and I believe that they were right in that. I quite agree with the argument made the other night by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) that inasmuch as the Provincial Legislature provides the machinery for enforcing such a law, that inasmuch as the administration of such a law must inevitably be with the Provincial Legislature, it is only just that the law should be passed by the Provincial Legislature.
There are other reasons in favour of such a course. Temperance legislation of this kind must inevitably interfere with rights that may be regarded as time-established, and there is no doubt that the citizens will accept from a Provincial Legislature more severe legislation in this regard than from any central legislative body. There are other reasons. In a country like Canada, with its vast territory, different conditions exist in different parts, and it is very much easier for a Provincial Legislature to pass an Act, which meets the particular conditions in a province, than it is for one Act passed by the Dominion Parliament which would apply to all parts of the Dominion. And it is very much easier to get amendments to an Act passed by a Provincial Legislature, and applying only to the province, than to get amendments to an Act passed by the Dominion Parliament. Therefore, I say that the temperance advocates in Canada have been right in the last sixteen years in devoting their attention largely, in the matter of reform,
to the various Provincial Legislatures. I think there is no doubt whatever that the proposals made by my hon. friend is the true solution of the problem, but the Macdonald Act, though very effective, contains this one provision:
It shall not affect, and is not intended to affect bona' fide transactions in liquor between a person in the province of Manitoba and a person in another province or a foreign country, and the provisions of this Act shall be construed accordingly.
That provision was necessary in the Macdonald Act to make it intra vires of the Manitoba Legislature, but that provision opens a very wide door, and it is that door which we propose to close by the proposals now before the House. I think there is very little doubt about the constitutionality of such a measure. My hon. friend from Prince county cited the opinion of the Attorney General of Manitoba, a very curious opinion I submit, and an opinion that seemed to he endorsed by the hon. member for North Cape Breton, that because the British North America Act contains a provision that the products of one province shall be deemed free to enter another province, therefore no such restrictions as proposed shall be placed on the statute-books.
When I want to ex press an opinion upon legislation I will express it not through the conduit of the hon. member.	[DOT]

I understood my hon. friend to come as near to expressing an inintelligent opinion on this as ever he does. As I have said, it strikes me that if that curious objection had any effect it would apply with equal force to a general prohibitory law. If we cannot, say that it is an offenloe to .send liquor into a province contrary to the laws of that province, we certainly cannot say it is an offence to send liquor into a province at all. So that, .notwithstanding the fact that it is credited to so high an authority as the Attorney General of Manitoba, and notwithstanding that it appeared to me to have the greater authority of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, I am inclined to attach very little importance to it.
It iseems to me that this is a proposition which ought to appeal to every member of this House, and I trust, for the sake of unity, that it will pass unanimously. It strikes me that seeing that this proposition meets everything that his resolution required, and



is in every way more practicable, the mover of the resolution, the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), who seconded the resolution, and who made a very effective speech in its support must agree that this is the proper solution of the problem. I believe that even the hon. gentlemen from Quebec who opposed the resolution will be inclined to favour this proposition. There was some difference of opinion expressed by the hon. member for Bonaventure and other members from that province as to the sentiment in Quebec. The hon. member for Bonaventure expressed the opinion that Quebec was in favour of prohibitory legislation, while other gentlemen said it was not. This proposition should meet either of those conditions. If the Province of Quebec is in favour of prohibitory legislation, my hon. friend frorrv Bonaventure with his very great eloquence, and with the influence he has at his command, can no doubt induce his friends, who are in power in Quebec, to place upon the statute books a prohibitory law. If the sentiment of Quebec is not as represented by the hon. member for Bonaventure, but is reflected by the other speakers from that province, we could hardly be justified in applying a measure to the province of Quebec against its wishes.
It strikes me that the prohibitionists in Canada are particularly anxious that whatever measure is placed on the .statute book shall be free from all possible criticism. It strikes me that they do not want to mix up this question with cross questions. I can conceive that if a Federal Act were passed applying to the whole of Canada, there might be substantial objections. I can conceive of the opponents of the measure arguing that so drastic a piece of legislation as this should not be passed by a Parliament whose term has nearly expired. I can understand them holding that a Parliament passing such drastic legislation should have a fresh mandate from the people of Canada. And certainly even an old Parliament is justified in saying that the province that enacts prohibition should be exempt from interference from the outside. I can conceive that the opponents of prohibition might say, with a good deal of effect, that to enact a federal law at the present juncture would be an interference with provincial rights. I can conceive our friends in Quebec saying that this Parliament waited until every other province bad committed itself to the reform of prohibition, and that fMr. Davidson.]
when they found that Quebec was not disposed to follow the example of the other provinces forced this measure upon that province. But the people of Quebec, by whom, I believe, provincial rights are very justly regarded as dear, can certainly have no objection to an Act which gives effect to provincial legislation, and which renders provincial Acts effective. If this Act were to be passed at the present time, and on the ground contained in the resolution that it is a war measure, I can conceive that it might be said to those who were in the habit of using intoxicants, it might be used by the Bourassas and Lavergnes, as an added reagon why this country should not have entered into this war. We do not want anything like that. We want to be united at this juncture. If this proposal is crystallised into leglislation we will have gone a very long way in a great reform. I believe we will have taken a step which will appeal not only to the people of Canada but to the generations which will inhabit this country in years to come. I think they will look back upon this amendment and say that the legislators of Canada, at a time when a foreign foie was knocking at the gate, were wise in regarding this as after all the greatest enemy of our country. I think they will commend us, that they will say that it is a practical and sound piece of legislation which protects this country forever against so potent arid dangerous an enemy.

Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to make any extended remarks on this question. As I represent a constituency in Saskatchewan I desire to say a few words with regard to some observations made by the hon. member for Calgary who did not appear to approve very much of some of the temperance legislation adopted by the Government of that province. Let me say, before dealing with this question, in regard to the province of Saskatchewan, that I appreciate very much the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary in moving his amendment in which he gave the history of the development of temperance legislation and the changed views of the people of Canada on the question of temperance. I can remember very well the passing of the Scott Act in the county of Huron from which I came. I have forgotten the year -I think it was in 1883-but it was passed by a considerable majority and some two or three years afterwards the same Act was

repealed by a very much larger majority. We all know that in various parts of the country temperance sentiment during the past fifteen or twenty years, and perhaps more particularly in the last three or four years, has increased very materially. It has been stated that in the province of Prince Edward Island they have had prohibition for a very considerable period of time. Very recently prohibition has been adopted in Nova Scotia. New Brunswick is about to adopt some prohibitory measure and Ontario is on the verge of adopting prohibition. In Alberta prohibition will come into force during the coming summer. Manitoba, very recently passed a prohibitory measure by a large majority. With regard to Saskatchewan, I do not know whether my hon. friend from Calgary intended to make any criticism of the Government of Saskatchewan but if he did I can only say to him that he seems to be very much interested in what has been done by that Government.

I merely made the observation that the liquor was sold by the Government in Saskatchewan in substantial quantities the figures showing sales up to $1,000,000. I did not make any criticism but I merely made that reference to Saskatchewan as a matter of interest.

I understood my hon.
friend to offer some criticism of the system of selling liquor in Saskatchewan. I so understood his remarks but I would be very sorry indeed to think that my hon. friend should direct any criticism at the selling of liquor by the Government of Saskatchewan.
I did not discuss that.

If that was not his intention I do not intend to discuss his remarks in that regard any further. When that legislation was passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan it was done practically at the request of the people who represented the banish-the-bar organization in the province, or the Committee of One Hundred. The Committee of One Hundred approved of that legislation. The idea was simply to banish the bar. Every person who knows anything about the liquor question knows that a great deal of the difficulty that occurs is the result of the sale of liquor over the bar. Young men meet together, and through the sale of liquor over the bar, become addicted to the use of intoxicating liquors. We all know that the bar has made many a confirntied "drunkard. The Government of
140*
Saskatchewan took hold of the banish-the-bar movement and it was the first Government that ever had the nerve to get up and say: We will banish the bar. They did banish the bar. What1 has been the effect? My hon. friend says that he did not intend to criticise the system of selling liquor in Saskatchewan. I must confess that I do not 'know what imy hon. friend meant if he did not wish to convey that impression. What has been the effect? My hon. friend says that within six months the Government of Saskatchewan, with twenty-three liquor stores-four or five of which were abolished by the people at municipal elections last December-sold $1,000,000 worth of liquor. I believe the figures are approximately correct. What would have been the situation supposing the bar had not been banished? Prom $150,000,000 to $200,000,000 has been the annual per capita consump-. tion of liquor throughout the Dominion of Canada. Saskatchewan has a population of a little more than half a million; we will take it at half a million. Take the average per capita 'consumption of liquor and take the population of Saskatchewan and you will find that the consumption of liquor in Saskatchewan would have been $20 per head or, for 500,000 people, $10,000,000 per annum. If they sell $1,000,000 worth in six months and another $1,000,000 worth in six months, you will have $2,000,000 worth of liquor which is only 20 per cent of the consumption that took place in Saskatchewan, taking into consideration the per capita consumption in the Dominion of Canada, during the year before the banish-the-bar legislation was put into effect. So that the province of Saskatchewan, in this present year, or from the first of July, will be some $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 better off than it would have been if the bar had still existed.
As far as this legislation in Saskatchewan is concerned, it was certainly a step in the right direction because it got at the very root of the evil and that is the bar. As far as the question of prohibition is concerned, II believe in it absolutely. I believed for many years in the proper enforcement of a proper license law and in some provinces the proper enforcement of a proper license Haw has worked out very well. But, insofar as any corrupting influences exist in connection with public life, the liquor men .are the men who are to blame for the large portion of those corrupting influences. The hon. member for Calgary says that we should not attempt to force such a measure upon the people of British Columbia, as they have not yet acted on the question. The only arguments the hon. member for Calgary has advanced are the two I have mentioned: first, that you should not force the views of one part of Canada upon another part, and, second, that you must he satisfied that there is a -tfell organized public opinion before you attempt to enforce a Dominion prohibition measure. Personally, I do not believe that we shall get total prohibition until the Dominion Government takes hold of the question and enacts some sort of prohibitory measure. It is quite true that the Act that has been introduced -and I understand that it is upon that Act that the hon. member for Calgary's amendment is based-is a step in the right direction.
