Mr. Speaker, I merely rise to make my position clear on this question. I am sure that the discussion we have had to-day and on the former occasion must have impressed the House with the fact that, generally speaking, hon. members realize that there is a great demand throughout the Dominion of Canada for some definite action along the line of dealing from a federal standpoint with the liquor traffic or the great temperance question. As regards the amendment proposed so eloquently by the hon. member for Calgary, had it been in the form of a separate motion, and not as an amendment to the motion proposed by myself, I cquld have approved it and given it very hearty support. But after having given the matter very careful thought, I can only conceive the amendment as a practical negative of my motion. Technically, this may not be so, but I must confess that the two suggestions are entirely distinct and apart. My proposals briefly were that the conditions arising on account of the war made it advisable, in the interest of the efficiency of the nation and of economy, that a definite step should be taken towards prohibiting indulgence in intoxicating liquor, and its ' manufacture and sale during the period of the war. The amendment, as I understand it, which reflects the terms of the Bill already introduced, is simply an ordinary Act giving some additional effect to the provincial legislation. I take this opportunity of congratulating the Government on the step so far as it goes. I think the measure is good from the standpoint of assisting the effectivity of provincial legislation, and so far as it does that, I certainly approve it.
I might be permitted to rrefer to one or two arguments advanced as to why we should accept provincial unit rather than the Dominion-wide unit. It has been argued that the provinces have the powers of property and civil rights and that the British North America Act places under this Parliament matters of national importance. I submit that if ever there was a matter of supreme national importance, it . is this problem above all other problems with which this Dominion is faced. Therefore, I think that under the provisions of the British North America Act it can be and should be dealt with by this Parliament.

I have in my hand the War Measures Act, 1914, which contains powers which would enable the Government to deal with this problem, and while I do not ask that the proposals of the hon. member for Calgary or the Bill which is consistent with them should be disregarded or dropped-I think it would be a mistake to do that- nevertheless, I draw the attention of the Government to the powers given them under this Act, and1 if it felt that the time is not opportune to introduce special legislation of a Dominion-wide character to deal with this problem, then it 12 m. may be that, under the provisions of the War Measures Act, action could still be taken which would not interfere with the motion before the House. Section 6 of the War Measures Act states:
The Governor in Council shall have power to do and authorize such acts and .things, and to make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.
I say, in the interest of the defence of Canada, in the interest of the prosecution of this war successfully, such action should be taken. But it states further:
And for greater certainty-
It provides these two special cases: transportation, trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture of any or all goods. It distinctly has in view dealing with the suppression of the manufacture of anything detrimental to the welfare of the country or interfering in any way with the prosecution of the war. My contention has been that this is a war measure and that the time is opportune and the necessity grave for (the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale of alcoholic liquors in Canada. I have already suggested to this House and to the Government that the great distilleries of the country now used for the manufacture of alcohol should be taken over by , the Gevernment for munition and war purposes and operated by them as Lloyd George is operating and controlling the distilleries in the Old Country, thus overcoming that great difficulty , with which otherwise the Government might be faced.
I believe that this House is of the opinion that there is a widespread demand, an overwhelming sentiment throughout Cap-'ada in favour of this movement. I be-

Sieve that hon. members are convinced of it apart from their own individual feeling, and that they only hesitate o-n the question of method. While I appreciaate the efforts and the arguments of my hon. friend from Calgary and while I also appreciate very much [DOT] the distinct step forward in temperance legislation that his amendment contemplates and the Bill already introduced provides for, nevertheless I feel that, if I am to he consistent with my action of the 6th of March in proposing the first resolution, if I am to be consistent with my record for fifteen years, I shall be forced to vote against the amendment and to stand by the original resolution. I may say that I appreciate to the full the step in advance made by the Bill before the House.

When I accepted the honour of seconding this motion, I pointed out that I had voted against prohibition in 1898; that I had never before been a prohibitionist, but that we were now face to face with peculiar conditions. For that reason, I said that I was favourable to the request made by this important deputation which launched its patriotic appeal. I am amazed to hear a gentleman of the keenness of the hon. member for Calgary doubt the public opinion existing throughout the country on this question at the present time. The country was delighted some few days ago to see the province of Ontario, the largest province in the Dominion, put aside all its party divisions in dealing with this great question of prohibition. Is there a member from Ontario in this House who has any doubt as to the feeling of the people of Ontario on this question? Is there a member from the great western provinces, from Manitoba to the coast, who has any doubt about the feeling of the western provinces on this question? Is there a member from Nova Scotia, from New Brunswick, or from Prince Edward Island who has any doubt upon this question? I undertake to speak for Quebec. I say that if Quebec had a referendum to-morrow on this subject, it would be carried. I had the honour of submitting to this House expressions of opinion from some of the most distinguished men in Quebec. If we had a vote to-morrow we would be up against a big fight in the city of Montreal from the liquor interests, but public opinion in Montreal would vanquish it for the sake of the one great cause that we have at heart: to win this war. Why was this question brought before the House? I wish to read the last paragraph of the patriotic appeal which was signed by such men as J. R. Booth, W. C. Edwards, Judge Lafontaine, President de la ILigne Anti-alcoholique de Montreal, and others.	'
By one simple Act of legislation following the overwhelming sentiment of the country, Parliament can save millions of dollars of waste, can by one stroke enormously add to the productive wealth of the country, and do more to increase the power of Canada to help the Empire than by any other legislation it may enact; in helping the Empire it will benefit our own people.
Two hundred thousand young Canadians have left their homes, friends and all their business Interests to endure the hardships of war, to fight and if need he to die for the Empire.- Shall those left at home not do everything possible to strengthen their hands and help them to win? The little self-denial Imposed by such an Act will enable Canada to vastly increase her power to help.
Will our leaders, forgetting party and remembering only Canada and the Empire support such a measure? Canada awaits with confidence their answer.
There is the whole question in a nutshell. We have this year a Budget of $425,000,000, on the authority of the Minister of Finance. That Budget will reach $500,000*000 next year. We may have a public debt in this country of $1,000,000,000. Why should we waste $125,000,000 on whisky? What has impelled the people of Ontario to unite on this question? Why a majority in its favour of 25,000 in Manitoba? Why a clean sweep in Saskatchewan and Alberta? Why the adoption of such legislation in Nova Scotia by a vote of 28 to 3? Why has the Government of New Brunswick introduced a Government measure? Why have the people of Prince Edward Island asked that effect be given to their provincial legislation? Because we are facing a terrible ordeal; because we are passing through the gravest crisis in the history of our country. We have to face an unusual condition of affairs; no man can foretell exactly where it will lead us. We have preached national economy. Thirty years ago the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, one of the keenest intellects of this country, delivered a classic speech in favour of prohibition, at a time when the question was not of the national importance that it is to-day, and secured from the Parliament of that day a promise that when public opinion ratified the passing of such a law, such legislation would he enacted. Is there an hon. member in this House who doubts for one moment what the public opinion of Canada is to-day?	We have	heard	the hon.Minister of	Trade and	Commerce
appeal for	national	economy	and
for personal economy. I have read in this House appeals from Bonar Law, from Asquith, from Kitchener, all having the same import. " We are fighting Germany " says Lloyd George; " we are fighting Austria, but our greatest fight is against liquor." That is our position in Canada today. We have had' hardships imposed upon us; we should have greater hardships to bear before we win this war. No man wants to see the cause of the Allies go down in this conflict. We are pleading for national unity, for the bringing together of two great races in thi3 country, for a better understanding between s.'iem. The provinces have done their utmost. Ontario has acted; Quebec has acted through her municipalities. If she has not acted through her legislature it is probably because, as the hon. member for Rouville has explained, they have preferred ,in Quebec to leave the matter to be dealt with individually by each municipality. But the municipalities having spoken; 916 of them having adopted prohibition within their limits. Forty-four out of 74 local constituencies have adopted prohibition.

The hon. gentleman
has said that the legislature of Quebec thought it wise to leave legislation along this line tr the municipalities. Does the hon. gentleman think that the Legislature of Quebec has done wisely in that regard?

I do not agree with the Legislature of Quebec, but when this position was fallen three or four years ago, we were not under war conditions, as we are at the present time. IThose who made the patriotic appeal for Federal prohibition made it because Canada was in a peculiar condition. Does the hon. member for Fron-tenac approve of wasting $125,000,000 this year on whisky?
No, certainly not.

Is he desirous that we
shall have all the economizing and all the efficiency possible for the great task that is before us? How are we going to equip our 500,000 young men if we have barrooms awaiting them at every street corner? Ask the Minister of Militia; ask the officers in charge of the military organization in this country what the banishing of liquor means for the efficiency of the soldier. If you want to help Germany, maintain the liquor traffic; if you want to help the Allies, the best thing you can do is wipe it away.

Since March 6 last I have received over 150 petitions and resolutions from all parts of the province of Quebec, and they merely ask what is reasonable: give us a prohibitory measure during the war and for three years after the war.
The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has defended this amendment of his, which I admit, with the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), is a step forward in temperance legislation; but it does not meet the issue at all. We must have extraordinary legislation to deal with exr traordinary conditions. No man could have dreamed in 1911, when this Government came into office, that it would ever be called on to bring into this House legislation involving expenditures of millions and hundreds of millions of dollars such as have been supported cheerfully by the Opposition in this House. How are we going to face these, tremendous expenditures if we do not take the ordinary means of doing so, by national economy; and I think the best way we can do it is by introducing prohibition at once, especially at a time when prohibition is necessary. The hon. member for Calgary says that the provinces have gone to their extreme limit, that this Bill will follow and supplement the provincial legislation; that any infraction of provincial law will be followed up by this Federal statute, that the province will have power to take out a prosecution in another province, if liquor comes from that province. On the other side of the Ottawa river liquor depots will he established and liquor dealers will come from there and deliver in any house in Ottawa whatever liquor is desired. Would that be respecting the opinion of the city of Ottawa or of the province of Ontario?
You mean they will disregard the law?

They will disregard the law. Ontario has not the power to punish the importation of liquor into that province. It has power to prevent the sale of liquor, and that is what has been done. But we are asking to stop the manufacture, importation and sale of liquor.
The Bill before the House prevents the bringing of liquor from Quebec into Ontario.
I will not pose as .an authority, but I shall read an article from the Pioneer of Toronto, the organ of the Dominion Alliance.
That is not an authority any more than any one else.'
It is the authority of the temperance people. These people have a right to speak for the prohibitionists, and they are in a majority in Ontario.

They have a right to speak for themselves. Does my hon. friend think that those who are respbnsible for what is in the Pioneer are any better lawyers or better able to judge the constitutionality of a law than members of this House?

This article deals with the question of Dominion prohibition as compared with provincial prohibition. Referring to the prohibition adopted toy various provinces, and speaking of the great result in Manitoba, it says:
This prohibition will not be as effective as Dominion prohibition would be. A province cannot interfere with the shipping- of liquor to its own private citizens, from the liquor dealers of another province. No province has prohibited the private keeping or consumption of liquor. The Dominion Parliament cannot pass legislation to facilitate any provincial prohibition other than what provinces have enacted. Therefore, the Dominion Parliament will not prohibit the shipping of liquor from a license province to private citizens in a prohibition province until the prohibition province prohibits the private citizen from having the liquor.
A Dominion prohibition law, however, would result in the suppression of such sale. The most effective restriction of intemperance must be by the Dominion law relating to the traffic in intoxicating liquor.
The one clear, straightforward course before the Dominion Parliament at the present time is the adoption of the resolution, moved by Mr. Stevens, and seconded by Hon. Mr. Marcil, declaring that the immediate duty is the enactment of a law to prohibit the manufacture, importation and sale of intoxicating liquor for beverage purposes.
Practically every province has approved this proposal. Even Quebec, although not doing so by a vote, has by the adoption of local option by-laws and by public expression of many prominent citizens, affirmed its readiness to support such a law. Quebec is not now an obstacle. The attitude of her representatives in the House of Commons sufficiently proves this.
When the Parliament votes for prohibition, it will be the duty of the Government to introduce a prohibitory Bill.
I shall not address the House at any further length; I wish merely to adhere to the position I first took. I was not formerly a prohibitionist and I have voted against prohibition; but I have been converted by 20 years' experience. I know what liquor means in this country. I have visited localities from which liquor has been banished, and where the people are to-day blessing the day it was banished. Liquor has been the curse of this country, as of every other. But we are passing through a tremendous ordeal, through a tremendous crisis. We have to face an enormous burden, the heaviest, possibly, ever placed on a nation of our size and population. We are willing to support that burden cheerfully but we want to be equipped as we should be, we desire that our soldiers should'feel that we of the great civilian army are doing something to bring about the great victory that our Empire has at heart, and I should be sorry, Mr. Speaker, if the vote that is about to be taken would be in any way dictated by party feelings or party motives, or would be on party lines in the slightest degree. How delighted Canada would be to-morrow to learn that the House of Commons had reiterated what it did in 1884 and in 1892, and declared in favour of national prohibition ! I am, Mr. Speaker, obliged to vote against the amendment.

have only a word or two to say on this question. I go further and say that it is the duty of this, or any other Government, to pass such legislation as will make it as difficult as possible for a man to be a bad citizen. When war broke out, if this Government had taken the position that the provinces should be consulted, and that we should wait to have the full expression of public opinion, what action would [DOT] Canada have taken?
We do not wait in this.
This is a war proposal, and you carefully avoid discussing it from that standpoint.
Why put forward your resolution as a war proposal?	*
Because we are facing an extraordinary' condition of affairs.

Does the hon. gentleman to say that that it is good to have prohibition in time of war, and that it is not advisable to have it in time of peace? Why put in that proviso at all? That is hedging. If there is ahy hedging being done it is by the mover and seconder of this resolution. The sentiment of the people of Canada is not in favour of prohibition merely because there is a war, but because they believe that the liquor traffic is .against the best interests of this country. What would be the result if we did not do that? Suppose that a province wanted to go only a certain distance in regard to prohibitory legislation, and this Parliament went beyond that, at once you would have a conflict of opinion between the province and the Dominion. When it comes to making the law effective, we have to depend upon the sentiment of the people of the provinces. go as far as you want to go in making your legislation absolutely effective. What more can any reasonable person ask for?

At this late hour it is not my intention to occupy more than a few minutes. I just want to express my sympathy with and support of the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). I am sure that every man in this House is perfectly well satisfied that the sentiment of every province in Canada is in favour of a prohibitory Act. All of us who have had anything to do with this question in the past, know that one of the great arguments against prohibition, whether by the Scott Act, by local option, or by provincial legislation, or in any other way, was that we did not have a real pro-

hibition Act, an Act that would cover the whole country, and that would permit the sale of liquor on one side of the road allowance and not on the other. If this resolution were passed by the Government and followed by an Act, it would meet the wishes of the great majority of the people of the Dominion. Most of the hon. members who have discussed the resolution have discussed it as a temperance resolution, while it is a war resolution first and foremost, which proposes to make prohibition last for the duration of the war, and for some two or three years afterwards during the time of reconstruction. The Minister of Finance has told us, and we all know, that we must economize. Here is a way in which the people of Canada can economize to the'extent of $125,000,000 or $150,000,000. How much easier it would be for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to get the revenue he required, if there was an extra $150,000,000 in the pockets of the people of Canada. There is no question that, as a war measure, prohibition .would be a great success. Why should the liquor men of Canada not make their Sacrifices as well as other people? There never was a time when this reform could be accomplished so easily as to-day. There is no unemployment to-day, and the men engaged in the manufacture of liquor could easily get other work to do. The distilleries and the breweries could be put to another use, and there would be no particular loss. This could be done more easily just now than at any other time, and the Government should have the courage to face the issue and face it squarely, and not try to side step it by a resolution such as that of my hon. friend the member for Calgary has introduced, to be followed by the measure of the Minister of Justice. That is only begging the question. If they would face the question fairly and squarely, I am sure they would have th6 support and approval of the great majority of the people of Canada.
I quite agree that the amendment of my hon. friend from Calgary is a step forward, and a step in the right direction. He put up some very good arguments, with many of which I agree, but, as a war measure, his amendment does not compare with the resolution that is now before us. Look at what has been done in Russia since the war began. They have abolished the manufacture and sale of liquor altogether. Look at what has been done in France, and in England, in connection with this matter, since the war started. Why should we in Canada be behind the Russians, and the French,
and the British? It appears to me that there is absolutely no reason why we should be behind them. I know that any one who has watched the working out of the law which has been in force in Saskatchewan since the first of. July last; would be glad to see a prohibitory law throughout the whole Dominion. I spent several months in the province of Saskatchewan, in my own constituency, after the law abolishing the bars came into effect, and I want to say that while travelling through my constituency, I did not see a single drunken man or one who showed signs of having taken drink. I do not mean to say that there is not a good deal of liquor being consumed there, because the Act passed by the Government of Saskatchewan is not a prohibitory Act, but is what the temperance people asked for. But you will find that before the end of this year every one of the Government liquor stores will be voted out of existence. Three or four of them were voted out last December by majorities of two to one, and by even larger majorities. That law is approved by the merchants and business men throughout the country, and any one who has seen it working, and the results that have flowed from it, would be perfectly well satisfied that the same law, if applied throughout the whole Dominion, would work well.
The result would be of great advantage to Canada, and of great advantage in winning the war, the object we have most in view. If this question were submitted to the vote of the people, as proposed toy the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver, I venture to say that 75 per cent of the people would support a proposal to abolish for all time to come the sale of liquor as a beverage. I shall have much pleasure in supporting the resolution of my hon. friend from Vancouver.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt at all in my judgment that the legislation contained in the Bill submitted by the Minister of Justice is a very considerable step in the direction of temperance legislation. Considered 'as a permanent measure it would, I think, meet with the approval of a great many people particularly since the explanation that I heard to-night from the hon. member for Calgary. It appears that the Bill will be more effective than I thought it would be and I presume it could be made more effective still in committee if improvements were considered necessary. At the same time, it does not seem to meet

the issue that is before the country. It has been -well pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver that his resolution is a temporary measure and ought to be considered in connection with the crisis the country is passing through in consequence of the war. Therefore, I would feel like supporting the resolution for that reason. But the hon. member for Calgary gave me another reason. He used- an argument that compels me to vote against his amendment. He emphasized very strongly that the voice of the rqajority in democratic countries must be heard. He said something like this: Once the voice of the democracy demands that I shall do without whiskey, that voice must be obeyed. Anybody must be convinced that the overwhelming opinion of this country is in favour of prohibition during the continuance of the war. Therefore, the argument of that hon. member is absolute and convincing on that point. If public opinion is not to be heeded then we are allowing the minority to rule contrary to the argument made by the hon. member for Calgary. Further than that, the prohibition sought to be brought into effect under the proposed legislation will likely 'be delayed for some time for, notwithstanding the statement made by the hon. member for Calgary that it is well within the competence of Provincial Parliaments to pass legislation having the effect of prohibition and that full effect will be given to it by the Bill now before the House, yet there is a contrary opinion in the country. The Montreal Gazette, a newspaper that is careful in its statements, said a day or two ago that the legislation proposed) by the Government will give rise to very interesting litigation. If it is very interesting, it will be expensive, and interesting and expensive litigation will mean delay. For these reasons, if the matter is to come before the courts and before the Privy Council for final decision, there will be considerable delay. We know that the liquor interests are well organized, that they are wealthy and that they will be able to contest any legislation that is proposed if there is a chance of defeating it. In all human probability that is what will take place. For these reasons, and particularly for the reason advanced by the hon. member for Calgary, that the majority ought to rule, I have to vote against the amendment introduced by the hon. gentleman himself. He has supplied me with the arguments that compel me to do 
that. Furthermore, I will support on its merits the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver though I approve of the legislation proposed by the Government.

speechtext: The amendment having been carried, there is no vote on the main motion. If the amendment had been lost we would have to vote on the main motion.

I respectfully ask that the main motion as amended be put to the House. I submit that, when the main motion was first presented, it was discussed and an amendment was moved. A vote has been taken upon that amendment. The members who were not in favour of the amendment voted against it, but there may be many members who prefer the main motion as amended to no motion at all, and they are entitled to vote upon it.
. Mr. SPEAKER: The main motion is:
That, in the opinion of this House, at this time when the Empire is at war, the conservation of the wealth and the resources of the Dominion and the promotion of the efficiency of our nation would be materially aided by the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes, and legislation for this purpose should be enacted forthwith.
The amendment reads:
That all the words in the proposed resolution after the word " that " be struck out, etc.
That is to say: with the exception of the first word of the resolution every word is stricken out, and the amendment was voted in the affirmative. Consequently, in my opinion, there is no main motion before the House.
